Ideophones add a distinctive extra-high or extra-low tone: 'Zum zweiten weisen Ideophone, zusätzlich zu den drei distinktiven Tönen, einen distinktiven Extrahoch- oder Extratiefton auf' (p. 24, citing Bohnhoff 2010: 52). tn.quote: Tone is mostly lexical in Dii, and one or two tone(s) are attached to each syllable (not to the vowel!), such that a given tone must be pronounced on whichever phoneme it falls, whether consonant or vowel. Only a few tones are modified in given grammatical contexts. The Dii are conscious enough of their 3 phonemic tone levels ... that they've given each a name: ... Five or six phonetic pitch levels can easily be distinguished, however. ... But in this work, all 3 are distinguished: / ́ / for high (H) tone, / ̀ / for low (L) tone, with mid (M) tone unmarked.

3644.quote: All words in Jiwarli must end in a vowel, and all words begin with one and only one consonant. In general, stress (emphasis) falls on the first vowel of a word. 3650.heavy: Four-level scale (62): heaviest = closed syllable or syllable containing a long vowel or VV sequence, (C)VC / (C)VV(C); then open syllable with onset CV; then onsetless open syllable V; lightest = open syllable with schwa nucleus (C)ə. Accent moves to σ2 only when σ2 outranks σ1 on this scale.
3650.dflt: first syllable of the word ('the first syllable as the preferred accent location'); the same holds when both window syllables are equal in weight, and in all disyllables regardless of weight because a final syllable may not be accented
3650.prule: One accent per word inside a bisyllabic window at the LEFT edge: the first syllable is accented unless the second syllable is heavier than the first, in which case accent shifts to the second syllable; the word-final syllable is never accented, so disyllables are always initial-accented whatever the weights. 3653.prule: No word stress is described. Donno So is a tone language (H, L, <HL>, <LH>, rarely <LHL> on syllables) whose lexical melodies are culminative: every lexical stem (verb, noun, adjective, numeral) carries exactly one lexically H-toned syllable or mora, and after phonological rules a word almost always has exactly one H. The position of that H is lexical, not computable from syllable count or weight: verbs are /HL/ or /LH/ (preordained for obstruent-initial verbs, lexical otherwise); nouns and other non-verb stems are /HL/ (H on the initial syllable of nonmonosyllabics), /LHL/, or /LH/ (tone break as far right as possible, on the final mora of a bimoraic final syllable); no /HLH/ and no all-/L/ stems. 3654.dq: two tones high (ˉ) and rising (´) are distinctive, functioning as a word-tone system. Only the first two syllables of words are tone bearing units (TBU).

An apostrophe (’) appearing between first and second syllables denotes that the second syllable is out of TBU and atonal.

3654.tone: The 2018 wordlist (p. 82-83) describes a two-way word-tone contrast, high (ˉ) vs rising (´), with the TBU limited to the first two syllables and later syllables atonal (low level); an apostrophe marks an 'accent nucleus' after syllable 1 that puts syllable 2 outside the TBU. The identical paragraph is printed for Lamo (§2.1) and Larong sMar (§2.2). Suzuki et al. 2024 (p. 67) call Drag-yab sMar's sister Lamo 'a tone language with a two-way distinction between H (high) and L (low) just like its sister languages, Larong sMar and Drag-yab sMar', analyse the system as word-initial H/L register plus an optional accent nucleus (falling point), and liken it to Kansai (Keihan) Japanese rather than to Tibetic; p. 79 (said of Lamo): a single-syllable stress-accent analysis (Caplow 2016a, b) 'has not been applied to Lamo; no linguistic realisation supports either the existence or non-existence of stress on a single syllable.' Table 4 (p. 78) gives numeral tone patterns for the mBengo, Razi and rDzongsar dialects of Drag-yab sMar (e.g. 'one' LH/L/L, 'two' H/H/L, 'ten' LH). Stress is explicitly non-contrastive ('बलाघातले अर्थमा भिन्नता ल्याउँदैन'); intonation is contrastive (statement = falling, polar question = rising, exx. 33-34). Nagila 2009 (Nepalese Linguistics 24) likewise describes only a question-final upglide, no lexical tone.
